1.explanation: All of the Handlebars highlighting logic lives inside the default‐exported function in src/languages/handlebars.js. Within its returned `contains` array there’s a mode object intended to match `{{else}}` blocks (using begin: /\{\{(?=else\}\})/). Because that regex only matches `{{else}}` immedi­ately followed by `}}`, it never sees `{{else if …}}` and so the branch isn’t tokenized as a template tag. Tweaking that mode (or adding a separate one for `else if`) inside the export default function will fix the broken rendering.
1.bug_scenario: The screenshot shows a Handlebars block `{{#if this.userData.isLoaded}}…{{else if this.userData.isError}}…{{/if}}` where the `else if` branch is not being recognized or highlighted correctly. The highlighter only picks up the opening `#if` and closing `{/if}` but fails to treat `{{else if …}}` as a template-tag, so keywords and values inside that branch aren’t styled distinctively.

2.explanation: Both of these default-export functions build the Highlight.js grammar for Handlebars/HTMLBars. The main Handlebars definition (in src/languages/handlebars.js) contains the keyword lists (BUILT_INS) and block-opening rules (OPENING_BLOCK_MUSTACHE_CONTENTS and the special “else” rule) that control how “if” and “else if” are recognized and colored. Because “else if” isn’t matched by the existing /{{(?=else\}\})/ rule and ‘else’ isn’t in the BUILT_INS, the conditional branches and path segments fall back to the generic template-variable mode. Any fix must update this grammar—adding “else” (and “else if”) to the keyword lists or expanding the block-opening regex—in src/languages/handlebars.js. The htmlbars.js stub then reuses that definition, so its default export also needs to pick up the corrected grammar.
2.bug_scenario: The screenshot shows a Handlebars/HTMLBars template with a standard block “if/else if” statement not being highlighted correctly. The “#if” and “/if” delimiters get one color, but the “else if” line and the path expressions (e.g. this.userData.isLoaded, this.userData.value.userName, this.userData.isError) are rendered inconsistently—with keywords, helper names, and values all using the same or wrong styles instead of distinguishing ‘if/else’ keywords from property paths.
